For one water cannot be like another; some are sweet, others are impregnated with salt and alum, others flow from hot springs. With respect to Radishes.—The Greek name ῥαφανὶς is derived from ῥᾳδίως φαίνεσθαι, because they quickly appear above ground; and in the plural the Attic writers either shorten or lengthen the penultima at pleasure. Cratinus writes— ταῖς ῥαφανῖσι δοκεῖ, it is like radishes, but not like other vegetables; and Eupolis, on the other hand, says— ʽῥαφανίδες ἄπλυτοι, unwashed radishes and cuttle-fish. For the word ἄπλυτοι, unwashed, must clearly refer to the radishes, and not to the cuttle-fish; as is shown by Antiphanes, in whom we find these lines:— To eat ducks, and honeycombs of wild bees, and eggs, And cheese-cakes, and unwash'd radishes, And rape, and oatmeal-groats, and honey. So that radishes appear to have been particularly called un- washed radishes; being probably the same as those called Thasian. Pherecrates says— There one may have the unwash'd radish, and the warm Bath, and closely stewed pickles, and nuts. And Plato, in his Hyperbolus, says, using the diminutive termination, φύλλιον ἤ ῥαφανίδιον, a leaflet, or a little radish.
